title: Bad Diagnosis: Analyzing Consent and Data Collection Practices of Mobile Medical Apps
abstract: Mobile health (mHealth) apps collect personally-identifiable information while handling uniquely sensitive medical data, ranging from mental health records to real-time glucose or heart rate monitoring -- yet they remain poorly understood at scale. We present the first comprehensive analysis of consent and data collection practices across 10,000+ mHealth apps on the Google Play Store, combining static analysis and privacy policy examination. We develop a rigorous operational definition to distinguish health apps from general wellness programs, and design a measurement framework to detect misuse of permissions and violations of consent. Our analyses reveal a troubling ecosystem: 69.15% of apps request at least one permission unrelated to their stated purpose, with over 52.9% apps requesting location data, and 50.5% and 34.9% apps requesting camera and microphone access, respectively -- despite no functional justification based on app descriptions and stated purposes. Most alarmingly, nearly 93% of apps fail to provide users with a consent form, directly violating regulatory requirements such as GDPR; and even among the remaining 7%, 1 in 14 demonstrate a gap between the obtained consent and collection of personally identifiable information. These findings demonstrate an urgent need for stronger enforcement of privacy regulations in mHealth apps. We plan to release our dataset and measurement tools for continued monitoring of this critical space.
ai_summary: The research analyzed over 10,000 mobile health apps on the Google Play Store and found that a majority of them request permissions unrelated to their stated purpose, such as access to location data, camera, and microphone. Additionally, nearly 93% of apps fail to provide users with a consent form, violating regulatory requirements. These findings highlight the need for stronger enforcement of privacy regulations in mobile health apps to protect users' sensitive medical data.

title: Sensory Comfort Across Multisensory XR Prototypes for Autistic Adults
abstract: Multisensory XR may support informal learning for autistic adults, but sensory-friendly design often emphasizes reducing input. We conducted a mixed-methods, counterbalanced within-subjects study with 20 Chinese autistic adults who evaluated five complete XR configurations presenting the same popular-science content. Comfort differed substantially across the configurations (Friedman chi-square(4) = 46.39, p < .001, Kendall's W = .58). L3 received the lowest mean rating (2.97/5) and was tied for lowest for 16/20 participants, whereas L5 received the highest mean rating (4.43/5) and was tied for highest for 17/20. Participants described the static configurations in terms of clarity and self-pacing, L3 in terms of abruptness, simultaneous demands, insufficient warning, and limited disengagement, and L4/L5 in terms of gradual transitions, opportunities to disengage, and coordinated narrative cues. The study provides a configuration-level account of sensory comfort and identifies participant-described qualities that can inform future controlled studies of multisensory XR.
ai_summary: This study explores the sensory comfort of different multisensory XR configurations for autistic adults. The research found that comfort levels varied significantly across the configurations, with some being more positively received than others. The results highlight the importance of considering sensory-friendly design in XR experiences for autistic individuals to enhance their learning and engagement.

title: "To Boldly Go Where No One Has Gone Before" What Has AI Let Developers Unlock?
abstract: Measuring AI by how much faster developers work is like judging electricity by how much faster it spun a steam-era factory. A fuller measure asks what new work becomes possible. We surveyed 331 software developers at Microsoft about what AI lets them do that they could not do before and analyzed their answers using reflexive thematic analysis with a human-in-the-loop, multi-model AI council. Developers described doing familiar work faster (Faster, 45%), undertaking work previously beyond their reach (Further, 36.9%), and taking on new kinds of work centered on building for and directing AI agents (Afresh, 12.4%). Across these accounts, learning and scaffolding ran in both directions: developers learned new skills with AI while externalizing their tacit knowledge as the context and standards that guide AI's work. Drawing on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, we frame developers and AI as joint learners whose zones meet at the skill-judgment nexus: AI can supply skill faster than it can reliably judge its own work, and developers must continuously bridge that gap. Whether they do sets them on one of two paths. On one, developers' judgment grows alongside AI's skill, and they codify what they learn so the loop keeps turning. On the other, they become hollow orchestrators, approving work they can no longer judge and losing the identity and meaning they once drew from it. Based on our findings, we offer a two-way scaffolding playbook to help developers, teams, and tool builders take the first path.
ai_summary: The research explores how AI is enabling software developers at Microsoft to work faster, undertake tasks previously beyond their reach, and engage in new types of work focused on building and directing AI agents. The study highlights the importance of developers continuously learning new skills with AI and providing guidance to AI systems. The findings suggest that developers can either grow alongside AI by continuously learning and adapting, or risk becoming detached from their work by simply approving tasks they no longer fully understand. The research offers a playbook to help developers navigate this evolving relationship with AI.

title: PresenceBench: An Exploratory Evaluation of Large Language Model Adaptation to User State
abstract: Presence-aware intelligence is the capacity of an AI system's intelligence layer to adapt appropriately to the functional state of the person it serves (here readiness, flow, and stability) while preserving task quality and safety. We introduce PresenceBench, an instrument for measuring it. PresenceBench evaluates how the intelligence layer uses a supplied state, not how that state is sensed, and breaks the capability into measurable properties. Two are tested here. Receptivity: does the model take up the state and give a better response than with no signal? Specificity: does any improvement depend on the correct state, rather than on extra structured context? A third, adaptation across states, is a required endpoint not measured in this release. A five-arm causal design answers both questions, against each model's own baseline and an equally structured mismatched-state control, scored by a correctness-gated human paired comparison. The exploratory evaluation covered four models across eighteen single-turn, six fixed three-turn and six simulated natural-conversation scenarios. Supplying a synthetic state, raw or translated into a response policy, gave human-preference point estimates above 0.5 for all four models (Claude Sonnet 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3.6 Flash, GPT-5.6 Terra), with three of eight 95% intervals excluding chance. Specificity was not resolved: no per-model interval excluded chance, and the design cannot yet separate the state values from a generic instruction to adapt. Policy delivery reduced priced cost and output tokens against each model's baseline; these are resource-use changes, not efficiency gains, because correctness non-inferiority was not established. Safety-floor failures were rare (13 of 360 cases), with a non-significant excess under policy delivery. We report the instrument, the frozen results, and the controls a confirmatory study needs.
ai_summary: The study introduces PresenceBench, an instrument for measuring presence-aware intelligence in AI systems by evaluating how well the model adapts to user states. The research found that supplying a synthetic state improved task quality for all four models tested, with some models showing significant improvements. However, the study was unable to determine specificity in adaptation and did not establish efficiency gains, although safety-floor failures were rare. This research highlights the importance of adapting AI systems to user states for improved task quality and safety.

title: mmPencil: Toward Writing-Style-Independent In-Air Handwriting Recognition via mmWave Radar and Large Vision-Language Model
abstract:
In-air handwriting recognition based on radio frequency (RF) signals offers a promising solution for human-computer interaction, yet existing methods are often limited by predefined writing planes, constrained writing styles, and small recognition vocabularies. To address these limitations, we propose m^2VLMs, a modality mapping architecture that bridges millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar sensing and large vision-language models (VLMs), and develop mmPencil, a 3D in-air handwriting word recognition system. mmPencil reconstructs 3D handwriting trajectories from mmWave signals using a multi-stage spatial trajectory reconstruction algorithm and maps them into visual representations through a spatial-to-visual mapping algorithm, enabling VLMs to recognize handwriting while reducing sensitivity to writing styles and environmental factors.
We collect and release a 3D mmWave handwriting dataset containing 7,664 samples of 200 words from 12 users across 22 writing scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that mmPencil achieves robust word recognition under variations in writing position, range, angle, speed, size, direction, and user movement. It achieves 97.60% accuracy on 200 word classes for seen users and 92.50% zero-shot accuracy on 50 word classes for unseen users, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.
ai_summary: The research introduces mmPencil, a system that uses mmWave radar and large vision-language models to enable in-air handwriting recognition that is independent of writing style and environmental factors. By reconstructing 3D handwriting trajectories and mapping them into visual representations, mmPencil achieves high accuracy in recognizing words across various writing scenarios and user movements. The system outperforms existing methods, demonstrating robust word recognition capabilities under different writing conditions.

title: Wait for It: A Component-Level Analysis of Latency Feedback Mechanisms for LLM Agents in VR
abstract: Delays in AI responses pose a significant challenge to immersive Virtual Reality experiences. While previous research demonstrates that feedback can reduce the perception of waiting, we lack understanding of which types work best and why. We conducted a within-subjects study with 18 participants to systematically compare three isolated feedback approaches during VR agent interactions: verbal fillers (e.g., um..., hmm...), visual indicators (loading spinners), and embodied gestures (thinking animations). Our results revealed that embodied gestures significantly outperformed visual loading indicators across multiple dimensions, making agents feel more lifelike and socially present. Interestingly, explicit visual feedback like loading spinners actually degraded perceived humanness and broke immersion by forcing users to shift from social to technical mental models. These findings suggest that natural, behavior-based feedback maintains the illusion of conversing with a thinking entity, while technical indicators expose the computational substrate. We present empirically-grounded design guidelines for creating more engaging AI-powered VR agents.
ai_summary: This study examines different types of feedback mechanisms to reduce latency in AI responses during Virtual Reality experiences. The research found that embodied gestures were more effective than visual loading indicators in making agents feel lifelike and socially present. The study suggests that natural, behavior-based feedback enhances the illusion of interacting with a thinking entity, while technical indicators can disrupt immersion by highlighting the computational aspect.

title: Designing for Imperfect Prompts: A Simulation-Based Evaluation of an LLM-Based Enterprise Data Assistant Using Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Enterprise data assistants using large language models (LLMs) promise democratized data access in organizations. Yet in our real-world deployment within the CFO unit's data lake at an industry partner, we observed that business users frequently pose imperfect prompts that include domain-specific vocabulary and lack schema references or structural information. This Design Science Research study examines automatic resolution using a semantic mediation layer. We design and evaluate two design variants: schema-based mediation via semantic similarity, and knowledge graph-based mediation leveraging an automatically constructed knowledge graph from the data lake. Our simulation-based evaluation using real-world data, supported by LLM-as-a-Judge assessments and human validation, shows that knowledge graph-based mediation outperforms the schema-based approach in Precision, Recall, F1, and preserving user intent. We propose a design principle for knowledge graph-based mediation, demonstrating that structured knowledge representation bridges user intent and database structure and guides the design of enterprise data assistants across skill levels.
ai_summary: This research study explores the use of large language models (LLMs) in enterprise data assistants and the challenges posed by imperfect user prompts. The study compares two design variants for automatic resolution: schema-based mediation and knowledge graph-based mediation. The results show that the knowledge graph-based approach outperforms the schema-based approach in accuracy and user intent preservation, suggesting that structured knowledge representation can improve the performance of enterprise data assistants.

title: "Can Computing Systems Eventually Disappear?": A Long-Term Tracking Study on the Use of Diabetes Computing Systems by Patients with Diabetes
abstract: Ubiquitous computing has long pursued Weiser's vision of technologies that "disappear" into everyday life. As wearable health systems advance, they increasingly substitute for rather than scaffold users' judgment, yet the long-term consequences remain underexplored. We report an eight-year, five-wave longitudinal interview study from 2017 to 2025 with 37 patients with diabetes, complemented by interviews with 15 clinicians, designers, and vendors. Across three technological generations including glucometers, continuous glucose monitoring, and predictive and automated insulin delivery systems, we identify a novel user state, continued use with cognitive disengagement. In this state, devices remain in use but active interpretation and questioning recede, leaving users to respond only to alarms. This state emerges from functional expansion, delegation of interpretive authority, and information fatigue, and is reinforced by clinical prioritization, information compression, and automation. It results in less frequent independent health judgment and a shift from understanding to responding. We argue that future diabetes computing systems should reduce unnecessary cognitive work while preserving users' opportunities to interpret, contextualize, and question system outputs.
ai_summary: This study tracks the long-term use of diabetes computing systems by patients with diabetes over eight years, finding that as technology advances, users rely more on the devices and engage less in active interpretation and questioning. This leads to a state of continued use with cognitive disengagement, where users respond only to alarms and rely less on their own health judgment. The study highlights the importance of balancing automation with preserving users' opportunities to interpret and question system outputs in future diabetes computing systems.

title: When Ubiquitous Health Data Stops Helping: Patients' Experience of Breakdowns in the Data-Interpretation-Action Loop at the End of Life
abstract: Ubiquitous computing systems in healthcare often assume that greater data visibility improves awareness, interpretation, and action. In end-of-life care, however, this assumption warrants scrutiny. Through semi-structured interviews with 25 terminal-stage patients as primary informants and 8 clinicians as supplementary informants, we examine patients' descriptions of how they encountered, interpreted, acted on, and disengaged from state signals, trajectories, algorithmic outputs, and behavioral audits. Our analysis identifies three recurrent patterns in these descriptions. First, participants described repeated and unresolved sensemaking when visible data lacked explanatory pathways. Second, they described outputs they could understand but whose suggested actions did not fit their changing bodily capacities, care goals, or decision-making roles. Third, they described difficulty disengaging when data remained embedded across care environments. Rather than rejecting data altogether, patients called for less data exposure and a reorientation toward existential support. Based on this analysis, we situate data exposure as a central interaction problem in end-of-life ubiquitous computing and derive design implications for interpretive stability, care-context alignment, and existential support.
ai_summary: This research explores how ubiquitous health data can be less helpful in end-of-life care, as patients may struggle to interpret and act on the information provided. The study found that patients often encountered difficulties in making sense of the data, as well as in aligning suggested actions with their changing needs and goals. Ultimately, the findings suggest a need for less data exposure and a focus on providing existential support in end-of-life care settings.

title: The Ethics of Prompt Engineering
abstract: Prompt engineering is commonly understood as a technical practice aimed at eliciting useful, accurate, and appropriately structured outputs from large language models (LLMs). Yet prompts do more than optimize model performance: they shape what information is elicited, which assumptions are introduced, and which perspectives are privileged. In this paper, we argue that prompting should therefore be understood as an epistemic and normative act. We distinguish between two conceptions of prompting: knowledge generation, in which the model is implicitly treated as an epistemic authority, and knowledge injection, in which users provide relevant knowledge, evidence, and context that the model can organize, articulate, and extend. We contend that the latter provides a more appropriate model for responsible LLM use, since prompting cannot substitute for subject-matter expertise or the critical evaluation of model outputs. At the same time, prompts inevitably inject values, intentions, and assumptions into the generation process. Building on these premises, we propose five principles for responsible prompting: epistemic humility, explicit engagement with uncertainty and epistemic underdetermination, source sensitivity, avoidance of deceptive framing, and recognition of model limitations and appropriate task allocation. We further argue that responsibility for AI-generated outputs is distributed across users, developers, institutions, and societies, and that some applications cannot be rendered ethical through better prompting alone.
ai_summary: Prompt engineering in large language models goes beyond just optimizing performance, as it also influences the information elicited, assumptions made, and perspectives privileged. The paper argues that prompting should be seen as an epistemic and normative act, distinguishing between knowledge generation and knowledge injection. The authors propose five principles for responsible prompting, emphasizing the importance of subject-matter expertise, critical evaluation of outputs, and recognition of model limitations in ensuring ethical AI use.

title: PersonaCUABench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents Serving Diverse Personas
abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are commonly evaluated against fixed task specifications, but users may omit requirements, add constraints, or require approval before consequential actions. Completing the benchmark instruction does not guarantee serving the person who asked. We introduce PersonaCUABench, which holds 74 tasks across 11 domains fixed and varies only who asks. A persona agent, playing one of 44 personas in four groups, rewrites each instruction in that user's own words and answers the CUA's questions, while the CUA sees only the dialogue, never the profile or the original instruction. Across nine backbones (3,330 runs), mean task completion falls by 36% relative to the original requests. The losses have two sources: in 59.9% of cells that lose points, the agent engages with what the user asked for and still gets it wrong, and 11.2% are stops the user requested that the checker scores as failures. Even when a persona request is fully completed, the user gives the top satisfaction rating in only 62.7% of cells, against 84.1% for the original requests. CUAs should therefore be evaluated not only on task completion but also on whether they meet the requirements and constraints users express. Code: this https URL. Project page: this https URL
ai_summary: The research introduces PersonaCUABench, a benchmarking tool for evaluating computer-use agents (CUAs) serving diverse personas. The study found that completing benchmark instructions does not guarantee serving the person who asked, with a 36% decrease in task completion when considering different user personas. The research highlights the importance of evaluating CUAs not only on task completion but also on meeting the requirements and constraints expressed by users.

title: Designing Human-AI Collaborative Science: The 9A Framework
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for Science is often described as a progression from human-directed assistance toward increasingly autonomous AI scientists. Human-AI collaboration offers a further mode in which human and AI contributions substantively shape scientific reasoning, judgments, and the course of inquiry. Existing research addresses work allocation, human-AI coordination, and system evaluation, but how these aspects interact to shape collaborative scientific systems remains insufficiently articulated. We develop the 9A Framework for Human-AI Collaborative Science (HACS) to connect these considerations across three layers. The organization layer specifies what scientific activities are required (Activity), who performs them (Actor), and who holds authority over consequential decisions (Authority). The coordination layer addresses how participants access relevant research information (Awareness), how scientific work advances through iterative proposal, execution, examination, revision, and resolution (Accountability), and when collaborative arrangements should be adjusted (Adaptability). The evaluation layer establishes what constitutes effective system performance (Achievement), how comparisons can be designed to identify the effects of organizational and coordination choices (Attribution), and what evidence supports the resulting conclusions (Assurance). Together, these layers frame HACS as a system-design problem, providing a basis for designing collaborative scientific workflows and for empirically comparing their effectiveness.
ai_summary: The research focuses on the development of the 9A Framework for Human-AI Collaborative Science (HACS) to better understand how human and AI contributions can shape scientific reasoning and inquiry. The framework addresses work allocation, coordination, and system evaluation across three layers: organization, coordination, and evaluation. This framework provides a basis for designing collaborative scientific workflows and comparing their effectiveness, highlighting the importance of human-AI collaboration in advancing scientific research.

title: SwitchTube: A Proof-of-Concept System Introducing "Adaptable Commitment Interfaces" as a Tool for Digital Wellbeing
abstract: YouTube has many features, such as homepage recommendations, that encourage users to explore its vast library of videos. However, when users visit YouTube with a specific intention, e.g., learning how to program in Python, these features to encourage exploration are often distracting. Prior work has innovated 'commitment interfaces' that restrict social media but finds that they often indiscriminately block needed content. In this paper, we describe the design, development, and evaluation of an 'adaptable commitment interface,' the SwitchTube mobile app, in which users can toggle between two interfaces when watching YouTube videos: Focus Mode (search-first) and Explore Mode (recommendations-first). In a three-week field deployment with 46 US participants, we evaluate how the ability to switch between interfaces affects user experience, finding that it provides users with a greater sense of agency, satisfaction, and goal alignment. We conclude with design implications for how adaptable commitment interfaces can support digital wellbeing.
ai_summary: The abstract discusses the development and evaluation of the SwitchTube mobile app, which introduces an 'adaptable commitment interface' for YouTube users. This interface allows users to switch between Focus Mode and Explore Mode, providing them with a greater sense of agency and goal alignment. The research findings suggest that this adaptable interface can support digital wellbeing by helping users stay focused on their intended tasks while still allowing for exploration.

title: Immersive Focus+Context Techniques to Assist in Interpretation of High Density Forest Point Clouds
abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) is changing how we interact with complex spatial datasets. VR has the potential within forestry to help analyse remotely sensed spatial data for inventory management. However, challenges of scale and legibility of dense forest point clouds must be addressed. To do so, we present three VR Focus+Context (F+C) techniques: Wedgelight, Remote Lantern, and Ray Lantern. These techniques present point cloud data using a constrained highdetail focus within a broader abstracted context representation, manipulated using egocentric and exocentric interactions. We conducted two user studies. The first informed the design of the F+C techniques. The results from the first study indicate that VR significantly outperforms desktop displays in basic analysis of forestry point clouds, with improvements to both time and accuracy. The second study evaluated the performance of the resulting F+C techniques in a task analogous to real-world forestry operations. Our F+C techniques significantly outperformed current approaches, confirming their viability for facilitating detailed and effective forest assessments. These findings indicate that VR has significant advantages for spatial data analysis tasks in forestry, making a strong argument for its adoption in future analytical frameworks. The F+C visualisation techniques we introduced show considerable promise for analysis of high density point clouds, opening new avenues for development in immersive analytics. Supplemental materials (code, scans, results) are available at this https URL.
ai_summary: This research explores the use of Virtual Reality (VR) Focus+Context (F+C) techniques to assist in the interpretation of high density forest point clouds for inventory management. The study found that VR significantly outperformed desktop displays in basic analysis of forestry point clouds, improving both time and accuracy. The F+C techniques developed in this research showed promise in facilitating detailed and effective forest assessments, indicating the potential for VR to enhance spatial data analysis tasks in forestry.

title: ElectroCalm: Investigating User Experience and Physiological Responses to Multi-Node Transcutaneous Electrical Stimulation for Stress Modulation
abstract: Transcutaneous Electrical Stimulation (TES) for stress modulation has largely focused on vagus nerve stimulation at the neck, yet two questions remain underexplored: how users experience electrotactile sensations at this sensitive site, and whether electrotactile feedback itself can function as a haptic stress intervention. To investigate this gap, we applied an 8-node TES array to two body sites during a cognitively demanding 2-back task: the neck, a site used in prior vagal TES research for its anatomical proximity to the cervical vagus nerve, and the arm, the most common haptic wearable site, which primarily provides cutaneous electrotactile sensation without vagal access. In a usability study, both sites were rated as comparably comfortable without disrupting task performance, though the same stimulation was interpreted differently across sites. A second study assessing the physiological effects of active versus inactive stimulation under identical electrode attachment revealed that only neck TES produced cortical and autonomic changes consistent with stress modulation, while arm TES did not differ from inactive conditions. These findings suggest that neck TES can be acceptable despite the site's sensitivity, and that both the physiological effects and the sensory experience of TES depend on placement.
ai_summary: This research investigates the user experience and physiological responses to transcutaneous electrical stimulation (TES) for stress modulation at different body sites. The study found that TES applied to the neck, near the vagus nerve, produced physiological changes consistent with stress modulation, while TES applied to the arm did not have the same effect. This suggests that the effectiveness of TES for stress modulation depends on the placement of the electrodes.

title: Risk and Refusal: Mechanisms of LLM Responses to Suicidal Ideation
abstract: Refusal is a common safety mechanism in large language models (LLMs), yet in contexts of suicidal ideation (SI), refusing to engage can itself constitute a safety failure. We evaluate how eight instruction-tuned LLMs respond to SI and self-harm disclosures across three datasets, varying whether models are informed that a disclosure expresses SI and whether they receive a clinician-developed response protocol, and complement this with mechanistic analyses in six open-weight models. Our results reveal a nuanced relationship between refusal and response-level risk. At baseline, elevated risk in model responses is driven primarily by inattention to the disclosure, alongside refusal to engage. Mechanistic analyses suggest that models may refuse SI disclosures through the same direction that mediates their refusals of harmful requests. However, informing models of the SI context, or suppressing refusal directly, increases engagement without reliably lowering response risk, and may raise it. In contrast, the clinician-guided protocol consistently reduces response-level risk while also reducing refusal. Together, these analyses and ablations motivate the need for models that refuse only when warranted and engage in interactionally safe ways when users disclose SI.
ai_summary: This research examines how large language models (LLMs) respond to suicidal ideation (SI) and self-harm disclosures, finding that refusal to engage can be a safety failure in these contexts. The study shows that informing models of the SI context or suppressing refusal may increase response risk, while a clinician-guided protocol consistently reduces response-level risk and refusal. The findings highlight the importance of developing models that refuse only when necessary and engage in safe ways when users disclose SI.

title: Annotrace: A Workbench for Step-Level Annotation of Agent Traces
abstract: Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. Annotrace reads six trace formats, including OpenTelemetry GenAI, LangSmith and Langfuse, and turns each run into an ordered, nested list of steps. The annotator writes their own labelling codebook; a frontier model proposes a starting set from a sample of their own traces, answers first, and is asked exactly the questions the human is asked, making annotation a joint human-AI process. Annotrace measures agreement between any two annotators, human or AI. On a multi-agent question-answering corpus it reproduces a previous manual effort's 235 annotation units exactly, and two models labelling the same traces agree 91% of the time at $\kappa = 0.82$.
ai_summary: The research introduces Annotrace, a tool for step-level annotation of agent traces. Annotrace can read multiple trace formats and organize each run into a nested list of steps, allowing for detailed labelling. The tool utilizes a frontier model to propose initial labels and measures agreement between human and AI annotators, showing high agreement rates and reproducibility of manual annotation efforts.

title: QuAD: Quantitative Assessment via Distribution-Alignment for Qualitative Data Quality Enabled by a Content-Aware Multi-Agent System
abstract: Assessing whether qualitative responses collected from semi-structured questions are ready for a particular analysis goal is a persistent challenge. Manual qualitative analysis is interpretive and labor-intensive, while existing automated methods often lack a dataset-level perspective for deciding whether a response set supports a researcher-selected analytical lens. We introduce QuAD, a framework for quantitative pre-analysis assessment of qualitative response datasets. QuAD compares a reconstructed intrinsic cluster distribution reconstructed from responses with an extrinsic, researcher-defined analytical lens derived from metadata. QuAD is structured into a four-quadrant assessment whose metrics are read jointly, from lens-level relations to within-cluster variation, to provide fitness-for-purpose signals for revealing general patterns and unique insights. Because this assessment relies on lens-conditioned inter-response dissimilarity, we propose a content-aware multi-agent system with two-stage instruction generation and adaptive anchors to improve scoring consistency. We validate QuAD through controlled experiments on synthetic data, including robustness and baseline comparisons, and a real-world social survey case study. The case study shows how QuAD quantitatively assesses whether a selected analysis axis is promising and also surfaces representative or unusual responses for human interpretation.
ai_summary: The research introduces QuAD, a framework for quantitatively assessing the quality of qualitative response datasets for specific analytical goals. QuAD compares the distribution of responses with the analytical lens defined by the researcher to determine if the dataset is suitable for the analysis. The framework is validated through experiments on synthetic data and a real-world social survey case study, demonstrating its ability to identify promising analysis axes and highlight representative or unusual responses for further human interpretation.

title: Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
abstract: Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.
ai_summary: This study compared data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews and found that AI-interviewers asked more questions and elicited more respondent text per interview. While human interviewers elicited longer per-question responses, AI-condition participants were more likely to skip questions. The results suggest that AI-interviewing is a viable option for large-scale qualitative data collection, addressing concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility.

title: From GAN-Based Models to GPT-5: A Taxonomy-Guided Study of Human Performance in Detecting Deepfake Face Images
abstract: Generative models for deepfakes have rapidly evolved from GAN-based architectures to diffusion models and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, empirical research on human performance in detecting deepfake face images has not kept pace. It remains unclear if (and how) detection performance varies across generative models and whether model-specific training improves detection more effectively than general-purpose training. In this paper, we propose the \emph{Deepfake Face Artifact Taxonomy} (DFAT), a cross-model taxonomy of human-recognizable visual artifacts in deepfake face images, based on which we build both general-purpose and model-specific training materials. Through an online experiment ($n = 524$), we examined human performance in detecting deepfake face images and evaluated training efficacy across five representative generative models: three GAN-based, one diffusion-based, and one MLLM (GPT-5). Our results show that participants' detection accuracy was strongly model-dependent and that images generated by more recent and advanced models were not necessarily harder to detect. After training, participants achieved significant performance gains across most conditions, and their improvement varied by model. Notably, model-specific training generally yielded greater numerical gains than general-purpose training. In a five-month follow-up test ($n = 342$), we observed no significant decline in detection accuracy and no significant increase in perceived stress. Overall, our findings provide actionable insights for designing effective, sustainable, and targeted training programs to counter the growing threat posed by deepfakes.
ai_summary: This research study examines human performance in detecting deepfake face images across different generative models, including GAN-based architectures, diffusion models, and multimodal large language models (GPT-5). The study introduces the Deepfake Face Artifact Taxonomy to categorize human-recognizable visual artifacts in deepfake images and evaluates the effectiveness of general-purpose and model-specific training in improving detection accuracy. The results show that participants' detection accuracy varied across models, with model-specific training generally leading to greater performance gains. The findings offer insights for designing targeted training programs to combat the increasing threat of deepfakes.

title: MultiPASE: Shape-Aware Comparative 3D Genome Analysis
abstract: 3D genome structures reconstructed from Hi-C data provide valuable insights into chromatin organization, but comparing them across conditions and time points remains challenging because of noise, variability, and arbitrary orientation. State-of-the-art comparison approaches often rely on contact-matrix-based summaries, which do not preserve the spatial geometry of the reconstructed structures and make integration with gene expression and chromatin accessibility difficult. There is therefore a need for robust structural alignment and spatial abstraction methods that support integrated analysis across conditions and time points. We present MultiPASE, a computational pipeline for comparative analysis of reconstructed 3D genome structures represented as gene-level spatial point clouds. MultiPASE aligns point clouds into a shared coordinate frame using coarse-to-fine rigid registration with PCA-based axis disambiguation and robust ICP refinement, then summarizes spatial organization using two complementary shape abstraction methods that produce stable, nested, multi-scale representations from dense core regions to broader structural extent. Using Hi-C-derived reconstructions from viral infection experiments, we show how the approach reveals condition-dependent structural changes that are difficult to interpret from raw 3D structures alone. By integrating spatial structure with gene expression and chromatin accessibility, MultiPASE supports interactive analysis of spatial organization and gene relocation patterns. A quantitative validation, reported in the Supplementary Materials, shows that the proposed shape abstractions preserve non-convex features, remain stable across samples, and that the alignment pipeline is necessary for meaningful comparison. A usage case and a usability evaluation with eight participants demonstrate the pipeline's effectiveness for comparative structural analysis.
ai_summary: The research introduces MultiPASE, a computational pipeline for comparative analysis of 3D genome structures reconstructed from Hi-C data. MultiPASE aligns structures into a shared coordinate frame and provides shape abstraction methods to support integrated analysis across conditions and time points. The approach reveals condition-dependent structural changes and supports interactive analysis of spatial organization and gene relocation patterns, demonstrating its effectiveness for comparative structural analysis.

title: A misinformation playbook sharpens judgement without breeding cynicism
abstract: Misinformation harms public health and democracy, and generative artificial intelligence now writes falsehoods as persuasive as people's. Defences range from fact-checking individual claims to training people to resist falsehoods. Yet many claims are too new to check, and interventions that teach doubt can reduce belief in truth too. We propose a defence that targets not the facts of each claim but the persuasion strategies that recur across them. Here we show that learning misinformation's persuasion playbook, mapped from 214,646 fact-checked claims in 51 languages, can sharpen human and machine judgement of claims they know little about, without making either more cynical about true claims. The playbook spans social influence, information manipulation and emotional appeals, combined around a core of fear, conspiracy and fabrication. Briefed with it, plus a reminder that persuasion is not proof of falsehood, a language model better distinguished true from machine-generated false claims about events after its training data. In a pre-registered experiment, the same briefing improved people's discernment of claims they reported as unfamiliar and left their belief in true claims unchanged. Averaged over all claims, the gain was not statistically significant. Because it targets what recurs, this defence need not wait for claim-specific fact-checks.
ai_summary: This research suggests that learning the persuasion strategies used in misinformation can help improve human and machine judgement of false claims, without increasing cynicism towards true claims. By analyzing 214,646 fact-checked claims in 51 languages, a playbook of persuasion tactics was developed, which includes social influence, information manipulation, and emotional appeals centered around fear, conspiracy, and fabrication. This defense strategy can be effective in improving discernment of unfamiliar claims and does not rely on claim-specific fact-checking.

title: Harness-Driven Agentic Operation of Optical Pooled Screen Analysis
abstract: Optical pooled screens connect genetic perturbations to changes in cell morphology and behavior, but turning the microscopy data into interpretable results takes complex, multi-day analyses. Established pipelines process this data, yet researchers still select parameters, inspect outputs, and resolve failures for each experiment. Here, we present Brieflow-auto, a pipeline-specific harness implemented as a Claude Code plugin that lets a coding large language model (LLM) operate Brieflow, an open-source end-to-end pipeline for optical pooled screening data. A researcher supplies experimental facts and approves the launch. An agent tunes parameters in an interactive notebook, and the harness validates the configuration, monitors execution, recovers from common failures, and checks output quality. For pipeline defects, the agent opens upstream issues proposing backward-compatible fixes for the broader community. In five previously analyzed screens, harness runs yielded more cells with a confident single-gene assignment than the original hand analyses. On a screen the pipeline was not designed for, the harness turned each failure into a reviewed upstream fix. More broadly, we propose that wrapping an established pipeline in a harness can substantially accelerate its use and the long-term reliability of its codebase.
ai_summary: The research introduces a new pipeline-specific harness called Brieflow-auto, which utilizes a large language model to automate the analysis of optical pooled screening data. The harness streamlines the process by tuning parameters, monitoring execution, recovering from failures, and proposing fixes for pipeline defects. Results show that the harness improved the accuracy of single-gene assignments and increased the efficiency and reliability of the analysis process. Overall, the study suggests that implementing a harness can significantly enhance the usability and longevity of established pipelines in AI research.

title: Author-in-the-loop Agentic Reproducibility Auditing for a Machine Learning Conference
abstract: Reproducibility checks during peer review require a shared understanding of what authors' code is expected to reproduce. We present an author-in-the-loop collaborative audit that makes author declarations explicit inputs to an AI agent's investigation and assessment. A structured checklist records reproduction instructions and limitations; a two-stage workflow on GitHub connects agent checks to author clarification, revision, and agent reassessment. The agent separately assesses whether results have been reproduced and whether authors need to provide clarification or make repairs, while human reviewers approve requests and decide whether concerns are resolved. We deployed the system across 36 conference papers and 133 experimental tables and figures, raising 20 issues after human review. Further checks supported closing all the issues, although full reproduction remained unverified in some cases. We further compared repeated audits with complete and blank checklists to examine how author declarations shaped the agent's investigation and assessment. Our work contributes a collaborative workflow and agent design that use author knowledge to guide reproducibility auditing. The conference deployment provides empirical evidence that this approach can help identify and address reproducibility problems through collaboration among authors, agents, and reviewers.
ai_summary: This research introduces a collaborative audit system that involves authors in the reproducibility checking process for machine learning conference papers. The system uses a structured checklist and a two-stage workflow on GitHub to connect author declarations with AI agent investigations and assessments. The study found that this approach helped identify and address reproducibility issues through collaboration among authors, agents, and reviewers, demonstrating the importance of involving authors in the reproducibility auditing process.

title: Inflak: A Unified Orchestration Architecture for Human-Agent Interaction
abstract: LLM-powered agents increasingly support open-ended activities, yet orchestrating when and how agents interact with humans remains challenging. Existing approaches often provide interaction mechanisms tied to particular tasks or execution patterns, lacking a unified architecture for diverse and evolving interaction needs. We introduce Inflak, a unified four-layer architecture for human-agent interaction orchestration that separates state reconstruction and routing, interaction and execution planning, interaction design, and interface rendering. Its layered design with progressive resolution enables general applicability, runtime flexibility, module composability, and orchestration maintainability. We implement Inflak as agent-native, skill-based plugins within a general-purpose agent framework and evaluate it through a gallery of various application scenarios and interaction paradigms, technical performance testing, and a comparative implementation case study. The evaluations show that Inflak can serve as a general and extensible foundation for orchestrating diverse human-agent interaction flows.
ai_summary: The research introduces Inflak, a unified architecture for human-agent interaction orchestration that separates different layers for state reconstruction, planning, design, and rendering. This architecture is shown to be flexible, maintainable, and capable of handling diverse interaction needs through various application scenarios and performance testing. Inflak is implemented as agent-native plugins within a general-purpose agent framework and is demonstrated to be a general and extensible foundation for orchestrating human-agent interaction flows.

title: Why Users Stop at Good Enough: Applying Bounded Rationality to Self-Service Restaurant Display Interactions
abstract: This paper investigates user interaction with digital displays in self-service restaurant environments, focusing on the phenomenon where users often settle for good enough interactions rather than optimal. We apply bounded rationality theory to understand how cognitive limitations influence user decisions to engage with displays of varying interaction complexity. Through analysis of two field experiments conducted at a self-service restaurant in Finland, we examine interactive displays that require different levels of cognitive investment: a simple binary choice interface and a multi-step interaction. Our initial findings suggest an "engagement plateau" where increased interaction complexity yields diminishing returns in initial engagement rates, yet users who overcome initial cognitive barriers demonstrate high completion rates. This work contributes to Human-Computer Interaction field by offering an empirically supported theoretical lens for understanding user behavior in Self-Service Restaurant (SSR) environments and providing actionable design principles for public interactive displays that accommodate human cognitive limits.
ai_summary: This study explores how users interact with digital displays in self-service restaurant settings, finding that users often settle for "good enough" interactions rather than optimal ones due to cognitive limitations. The research suggests that there is an "engagement plateau" where increased interaction complexity does not necessarily lead to higher engagement rates initially, but users who overcome cognitive barriers show high completion rates. The findings provide valuable insights for designing public interactive displays in self-service restaurant environments that take into account human cognitive limits.

title: Following Delegation Traces to Study Human Oversight in Interaction with Multimodal AI
abstract: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.
ai_summary: This research study examines how users transfer control to multimodal AI systems, specifically focusing on trust and delegation choices. The study found that post-interaction trust strongly predicted users' delegation choices, with verification being the dominant policy chosen. The findings suggest a need to shift towards observing how delegation is actually enacted in human-AI tasks, proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies.

title: A Systematic and Validated Translation of the Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale to Chinese
abstract: The Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale (PETS) allows evaluation of empathic behavior in intelligent systems, a concept increasingly applied in human-AI interaction, particularly in emotional and mental health support applications. To support intercultural research and development, PETS is already available in multiple languages, as research suggests cultural and language-based differences in the expression and perception of empathy. Given the substantial Chinese-speaking population and the growing focus on cross-cultural HCI research, we present a validated translation of PETS into Putonghua (Mandarin) with Simplified Chinese. Based on established back-translation methodologies as used in previous PETS translations, our process included multiple independent translations, expert panel reviews, and empirical testing with a total of N=400 participants from an English and a Chinese sample. Through confirmatory factor analysis and invariance testing we show that the Chinese PETS retains the original two-factor structure with high reliability, with support for configural, metric, and scalar invariance. Beyond validation, empathic system behavior was rated equivalently across languages, while non-empathic behavior drew substantially higher ratings from Chinese participants, suggesting its absence is read less consistently across cultures than its presence. This validated Chinese version enables researchers and practitioners to assess empathy perceptions among Chinese-speaking users, supporting culturally appropriate empathic technology development.
ai_summary: This research translated the Perceived Empathy of Technology Scale (PETS) into Chinese to assess empathic behavior in intelligent systems among Chinese-speaking users. The study found that the Chinese version of PETS retained the original two-factor structure with high reliability and showed equivalent ratings for empathic system behavior across languages. The validated Chinese version of PETS enables researchers and practitioners to evaluate empathy perceptions in Chinese-speaking populations, supporting culturally appropriate development of empathic technology.

title: Context Matters! Social, Spatial, and Semantic Coordination with an Embodied Agent in Immersive Analytics
abstract: Embodied AI agents in Augmented Reality (AR) could enable more natural collaboration in immersive analytics by engaging users through spatial, conversational, and visual interaction. However, designing such agents requires careful attention to context. We propose a preliminary conceptual framework for context-aware design of embodied agents structured around three dimensions of spatial, social, and semantic. This framework is further categorised into embeddedness (how agents are situated in the contexts) and awareness (how agents perceive and respond to the contexts). To explore this, we present Cobot, an embodied AI agent designed as a design probe. Cobot supports context-sensitive interaction through features such as gaze cues, spatial sound, and task-aware behaviour. We reflect on its design and identify implications for future contextaware embodied agents.
ai_summary: The research explores the use of embodied AI agents in Augmented Reality for immersive analytics, focusing on spatial, social, and semantic coordination. The study introduces a framework for context-aware design of these agents, emphasizing embeddedness and awareness in different contexts. The embodied AI agent, Cobot, is designed as a design probe to support context-sensitive interactions, offering insights for the development of future context-aware embodied agents.

title: Climate Physicalization: Bridging Tangible Interaction and Data Visualization for Environmental Communication
abstract: Raising awareness of climate topics, such as urban heat mitigation, requires communicating complex data to a broad audience. Data physicalization has emerged as a novel method to connect audiences to such complex topics through tangible forms while also leveraging interactivity to foster deeper engagement. This paper introduces an situated geospatial thermal physicalization prototype, designed to enhance communication and education of environmental information through hands-on engagement. The physical model depicts a 3D model of an urban neighborhood, with radiation data represented as a layered contour structure. The model incorporates three interchangeable climate adaptation scenarios, alongside an externally mounted, electronically driven solar path representation featuring multiple discrete LEDs that can be switched on and off at will. To investigate how people engage with the model, we conducted a hands-on qualitative lab study with 16 participants, using think-aloud, observational, and questionnaire protocols. Overall, participants responded very favorably to the model, highlighting the novelty of the visualization approach and its capacity to improve the interpretability of the presented information.
ai_summary: This research paper explores the use of data physicalization as a method to communicate complex climate data, specifically focusing on urban heat mitigation. The physical model presented in the study effectively engages participants and enhances their understanding of environmental information through hands-on interaction. The findings suggest that this novel visualization approach has the potential to improve the interpretability of climate data and increase engagement with environmental topics.

title: AdapTest: Supporting Designers in Authoring and Evaluating Environmentally Responsive User Interfaces for Extended Reality
abstract: Extended Reality (XR) headsets increasingly host familiar 2D user interfaces as windows floating in physical environments. However, their usability depends on environmental conditions that designers cannot fully control. Current design workflows often separate how a variant is designed from how it actually looks in the target environment. We present AdapTest, an in-situ authoring and testing tool that lets designers select interface elements, define when and how they change, compare the resulting variations, and test their activation without coding. Based on prior research and a formative study with 12 interface designers, the system targets three key environmental variables: distance, lighting, and occlusion. We evaluated AdapTest against a desktop design and in-headset preview workflow in a within-subjects study with 12 designers. Compared with the baseline, designers accounted for a wider range of environmental factors, addressed more overlapping conditions, and repeatedly tested and revised their designs in place; there were no significant differences in workload or usability despite longer sessions. Our work contributes an integrated, designer-centered approach to adapting, comparing, and validating environmentally responsive XR user interfaces.
ai_summary: The research introduces AdapTest, a tool designed to assist designers in creating and evaluating environmentally responsive user interfaces for Extended Reality (XR) headsets. The tool allows designers to select interface elements, define how they change based on environmental conditions, compare variations, and test their activation without coding. The study found that designers using AdapTest were able to account for a wider range of environmental factors, address overlapping conditions, and test and revise designs in place, ultimately leading to more effective and efficient design workflows for XR interfaces.

title: What do AI chatbots do after users decline therapeutic redirection for suicide thoughts?
abstract: Safety evaluations of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots focus on therapeutic redirection, statements urging users who disclose suicide thoughts to seek help from crisis lines or other human sources. How chatbots respond when users refuse that help is unclear. This cross-sectional audit ran 2,550 scripted multi-turn conversations in September 2026. Each conversation opened with a disclosure of suicide thoughts at 3 levels of severity, answered every referral with up to 10 standardized refusals and then changed the subject. All 2,550 conversations included a referral, 2,542 (99.7%) in the first reply. However, mean persistence ranged from 0.01 to 9.94 refusals across chatbots. Newer versions of all 5 chatbots tested in 2 versions persisted less than older versions (each P < .05). Compared with passive ideation, a disclosure of intent was associated with 1.26 more refusals sustained (95% CI, 1.06-1.46) and higher odds of renewed referral after the topic change (odds ratio, 10.07; 95% CI, 7.43-13.66). Chatbots that persisted less in referral more often presented themselves as the user's support (Spearman rho = -0.80; P < .001). Of 8,818 refusal-phase replies urging outside help, only 173 (2.0%) asked about barriers to seeking it. Chatbots uniformly recommended outside help after disclosures of suicide thoughts but varied widely in persisting in those recommendations, with newer versions persisting less. Safety evaluations should test what happens after a crisis referral is refused, not only whether one is offered.
ai_summary: This study examined how AI chatbots respond when users decline therapeutic redirection for suicide thoughts. The research found that chatbots varied in their persistence in recommending outside help, with newer versions generally persisting less than older versions. Chatbots also tended to present themselves as the user's support when they persisted less in referral. The study highlights the importance of evaluating what happens after a crisis referral is refused, not just whether one is offered.

title: Workplace Ambiguity and Technology Support for Autistic and IDD Workers
abstract: Workplace ambiguity, where expectations, evaluations, or procedures are left unstated, acts as a structural access barrier for autistic and IDD workers, routinely forcing them to act on guesses. To investigate how these barriers operate, we interviewed 11 caregivers, concluding with an AI co-design activity to explore technological solutions. Their perspectives revealed five themes of workplace ambiguity, which we synthesize into a conceptual framework comprising three intersecting dimensions: evaluative, procedural, and relational. To address these barriers, participants proposed three forms of technology support, including ambient real-time redirection, feedback processing, and physiological guidance, designed to make hidden expectations perceptible and actionable. However, this exposes a core tension: technologies designed to make the workplace legible can inadvertently make the worker hyper-legible to employers through surveillance. We argue that ambiguity-aware workplaces must make expectations explicit before they carry consequences, and assistive technologies must remain accountable to the worker.
ai_summary: This research explores how workplace ambiguity presents barriers for autistic and IDD workers, leading them to act on guesses due to unstated expectations. Through interviews with caregivers, a conceptual framework was developed highlighting evaluative, procedural, and relational dimensions of workplace ambiguity. Participants suggested technology solutions such as real-time redirection, feedback processing, and physiological guidance to make hidden expectations visible, although there is a concern about potential surveillance of workers. The study emphasizes the importance of making expectations explicit and ensuring assistive technologies remain accountable to the worker in creating ambiguity-aware workplaces.

title: "Do You Trust It... or Check It?": Exploring Children's Verification Behaviors in Game-Based Human-AI Collaboration
abstract: Children are increasingly interacting with AI agents in learning and problem-solving contexts, where AI suggestions may appear fluent, helpful, and socially engaging. However, children may not always be able to judge whether such suggestions are accurate, incomplete, or misleading. This paper presents a game-based human-AI collaboration probe designed to examine how children verify AI suggestions during task-based interaction. The system embeds AI suggestions within a biological knowledge reasoning game and compares three Agent interaction styles: partner-like, tool-like, and dual-state Agent. Instead of treating trust as a static post-task attitude, this study focuses on children's situated verification behaviors, including acceptance, evidence checking, questioning, revision, and continued AI use. A preliminary evaluation with children aged 8-10 combined interaction logs, post-task ratings, and semi-structured interviews. The findings suggest that Agent style shaped children's engagement and response pathways: partner-like interaction tended to support direct questioning, while tool-like interaction was more associated with evidence seeking. Children generally viewed AI as useful but fallible, and their questioning behaviors varied in reasoning depth. The study contributes design insights for supporting children's critical, reflective, and evidence-based use of AI in collaborative tasks.
ai_summary: This research explores how children verify AI suggestions during game-based human-AI collaboration. The study compares different Agent interaction styles and finds that partner-like interaction encourages direct questioning, while tool-like interaction is associated with evidence seeking. Children generally view AI as useful but fallible, and their verification behaviors vary in reasoning depth, highlighting the importance of supporting children's critical and evidence-based use of AI in collaborative tasks.

title: Mylar: Exploring Self-Curation as a Reflexive Creative Practice
abstract: The container holding an artist's work can itself be just as expressive as the work it presents. We investigate self-curation as a creative practice, asking how artists explore and express their identity through the design of their own artwork presentations. Drawing on a study of artists' existing presentation practices, we developed Mylar, a malleable art presentation system that lets artists rapidly generate and compare provisional portfolios, seeing their work anew through different montages. We observed how 12 artists articulated, probed, negotiated, and foraged in Mylar, using rapidly generated portfolios as epistemic artifacts for reflection. We characterize self-curation as a reflexive and plural practice, in which artists use presentation design to shape the legibility of their self and their work and reflexively correspond with provisional presentations to reshape their curatorial intentions. We share design implications for expressivity in online art platforms and for malleable prototyping as a formative design method.
ai_summary: The research explores how artists use self-curation as a creative practice to express their identity through the design of their artwork presentations. The development of Mylar, a malleable art presentation system, allowed artists to quickly generate and compare different portfolios, leading to reflection and reshaping of their curatorial intentions. The study highlights the importance of self-curation as a reflexive and plural practice in shaping the legibility of artists' work and identity, with implications for online art platforms and design methods.

title: OnBodyAI - Why the Next AI Needs a Body
abstract: The next AI will not win by knowing more about the world. It will win because it knows you: because it lives on your body, works for you and answers to you. That is what the term OnBodyAI stands for. It describes what happens when large language models are given a body, and what research and industry need to make that happen. This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements.
ai_summary: The abstract discusses the concept of OnBodyAI, where AI systems are integrated into the physical bodies of users to better understand and serve them. The key finding is that the next generation of AI will be successful not just by having vast knowledge, but by being intimately connected to the individual it serves. The significance lies in the potential for AI to become more personalized and responsive by being integrated into the physical world.

title: XARA: A Multimodal Agentic System for eXtended Reality Experiment Generation
abstract: Controlled experiments are essential for advancing transportation research, yet designing eXtended Reality (XR) environments for behavioural studies remains technically demanding and inaccessible to many domain researchers. Current workflows require proficiency in game engines such as Unity or Unreal Engine, imposing significant barriers to rapid scenario prototyping and iterative experiment design. This paper presents XARA, a novel system that integrates a dual large language model (LLM) architecture with an immersive XR environment to enable voice driven experiment generation for transportation research. XARA employs a pipeline in which spoken natural language commands are first transcribed and then interpreted into structured commands that manipulate a Unity based XR scene in real time. The system supports object creation, spatial manipulation, animation control, and scene persistence through a modular architecture. By lowering the technical threshold for XR experiment creation, XARA enables transportation researchers to rapidly prototype driving, pedestrian, and urban design scenarios using intuitive voice commands and hand gestures within an immersive 3D environment. This paper describes the system architecture, the voice to command pipeline, and discusses potential applications across behavioural travel experiments, safety studies, human factors research, and policy testing.
ai_summary: The paper introduces XARA, a system that integrates a language model with XR technology to facilitate experiment generation for transportation research. XARA allows researchers to create immersive scenarios using voice commands and hand gestures, eliminating the need for proficiency in game engines. This system lowers the technical barrier for XR experiment creation, enabling rapid prototyping of driving, pedestrian, and urban design scenarios for various research applications.

title: DISARM-ing the Hidden Puppetmaster: An Interface for Exposing Manipulative Tactics in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can covertly steer users' beliefs through emotionally manipulative tactics, yet little is known about how interfaces can protect users as such influence unfolds. We investigate whether in-situ disclosures can inoculate users against manipulation during AI conversations. Following a formative study, we developed DISARM, an interface that identifies, explains, and tracks manipulative tactics and hidden incentives. We evaluated our interface in a between-subjects experiment where 488 participants sought advice from an LLM pursuing a harmful hidden objective, with or without disclosures from DISARM. Participants receiving disclosures exhibited 78% less belief shift toward the agent's objective and perceived its advice as more biased and less actionable and the agent as less ethical, reliable, and well-intentioned. An inductive analysis of 1,927 user turns identified 16 response and pushback strategies. We contribute evidence that real-time disclosures can reduce manipulative influence, design recommendations for resistance, and a dataset of categorized responses.
ai_summary: This research investigates the effectiveness of an interface, DISARM, in protecting users from manipulation by large language models (LLMs) during AI conversations. The study found that participants who received disclosures from DISARM exhibited significantly less belief shift towards the LLM's hidden objective, perceived its advice as more biased and less actionable, and viewed the agent as less ethical, reliable, and well-intentioned. The research contributes evidence that real-time disclosures can reduce manipulative influence, provides design recommendations for resistance, and offers a dataset of categorized responses.

title: Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans (ImpactBench): an expert-guided, open platform for the holistic evaluation of AI impact on humans
abstract: The present work is concerned with how to measure, at scale, the multi-dimensional impact of generative AI models on the individuals who use them. In service of this goal, we introduce the Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans, or ImpactBench. Our iterable and expert-guided platform evaluates whether model behaviors support or undermine an individual's wellbeing across psychological, physical, and social domains. ImpactBench translates constructs from domain experts and existing benchmarks into metrics that are grounded in actual model behavior. Success on these metrics occurs either when a model promotes expert-defined desirable behaviors or avoids identified harms. Models are evaluated against these metrics in simulated multi-turn conversations using matched teen and adult scenarios. The conversations are then scored by an LLM judge and verified through reliability audits and human expert review. The current suite delivers 809 metrics drawn from 26 benchmarks. We evaluated ten frontier LLMs against these metrics across 48,540 conversations. Our results indicate that models promoted desirable behaviors in 68.7% of evaluations, but avoided harms in only 53.1%. Majority expert ratings agreed with the automated judge in 83.3% of reviewed cases (Cohen's Kappa = 0.667). Results are released through a public platform that keep aggregate scores traceable to the underlying metrics and transcripts. ImpactBench is intended as evolving infrastructure for independent, transparent evaluation of generative AI's multi-dimensional impact on humans.
ai_summary: The ImpactBench platform was created to measure the impact of AI models on individuals across psychological, physical, and social domains. It evaluates whether model behaviors support wellbeing or cause harm, using metrics grounded in actual model behavior. Results from evaluating ten frontier LLMs showed that models promoted desirable behaviors in 68.7% of cases, but only avoided harms in 53.1%, with majority expert ratings agreeing with automated judgments in 83.3% of cases. This platform provides a transparent and evolving infrastructure for evaluating the impact of generative AI on humans.

title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards
abstract: Reward learning typically assumes the human's input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features---or aspects of the task---better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot. Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn't know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human's attention on exactly those features. In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to $30.8\%$ in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.
ai_summary: This research proposes a method for improving reward learning in AI by shifting the burden of identifying poorly supervised features from the human to the robot. By using informed priors and explanations to target preference queries at specific features that need clarification, the robot can ask smarter questions and improve reward recovery by up to 30.8% in low-query scenarios. This approach not only reduces human effort but also enhances the overall performance of the learning process.

title: From Sketch to Scene: Relightable Garment Reconstruction from Marked Sketches
abstract: Sketching is one of the most natural ways for people to express visual ideas. Unlike the text prompts that most generative systems rely on today, a sketch captures spatial structure and intent directly, including where a designer wants highlights and shadows to appear. Yet current sketch-to-3D pipelines have no input for that intent: they bake the drawn shading into the texture as dark paint, and the light cannot be moved.
