We propose a system that transforms a rough garment sketch, marked with sparse annotations (a star for a highlight and a moon for a shadow), and a short text prompt describing the texture, into a textured 3D mesh with an explicit directional light, as a scene that can be relit and edited after generation. The two symbols are the most frequent proposals in an elicitation study with art students. From the marked sketch the system predicts the scene's directional light and, separately, a displacement field that bends the surface so that the moon-marked regions fall into shadow under that light, rather than being painted dark in the texture.
ai_summary: This research proposes a system that can transform a rough garment sketch marked with sparse annotations into a textured 3D mesh with an explicit directional light, allowing for the scene to be relit and edited after generation. The system utilizes symbols such as a star for highlights and a moon for shadows, which were found to be the most frequent proposals in an elicitation study with art students. This approach addresses the limitations of current sketch-to-3D pipelines by incorporating spatial structure and intent from the sketch, enabling more flexibility and control in the final output.

title: Kolab: Benchmarking Human-Agent Collaboration in Long-Horizon Workflows
abstract: When humans collaborate with AI agents on long-horizon tasks, what happens to the agents' contributions? For solving long-horizon tasks, humans place greater importance on ongoing interaction with AI agents (e.g., revising plans) than on an agent's ability to complete the task in a single attempt. However, most agentic benchmarks have focused more on automation. Strong performance on such benchmarks does not imply effective real-world collaboration. Professional workflows offer a useful setting, as they often involve interdependent steps. To address this gap, we introduce Kolab, a new dataset of 115+ hours of screen recordings of 50 professionals from 40 occupations collaborating with agents on realistic, long-horizon problems. Kolab also contains participants' collaboration and output quality judgments. Our analysis reveals diverse collaboration patterns, highlighting the importance of when and how professionals coordinate with agents. A collaborative agent must do two things that automation benchmarks never test: anticipate whether experts will adopt, modify, or reject its contribution once it leaves the chat window to guide its next steps, and assess collaboration quality from the unfolding workflow without constant expert feedback. Our benchmark operationalizes both: (1) forecasting how professionals use agent contributions at diverse workflows, and (2) verifying their judgments of collaboration satisfaction and output quality. Findings show that frontier models, both agentic and non-agentic, overestimate collaboration with experts and struggle to distinguish between high- and low-quality collaboration. Longer workflow context does not consistently improve these predictions. As frontier agents cannot yet understand long-horizon collaboration with experts, we position Kolab as a valuable dataset for studying human-agent collaboration grounded in real professional workflows.
ai_summary: The research explores human-agent collaboration in long-horizon tasks, finding that humans prioritize ongoing interaction with AI agents over task completion in a single attempt. The study introduces a new dataset, Kolab, containing screen recordings of professionals collaborating with agents on realistic problems, highlighting the importance of coordination and quality judgments in collaboration. The findings suggest that current AI models struggle to understand and predict collaboration with experts in professional workflows, making Kolab a valuable resource for studying human-agent collaboration in real-world settings.

title: EEG-Based Prediction of Music Enjoyment Using Deep Learning with Explainable Temporal Analysis
abstract: Understanding why listeners enjoy music is difficult because the experience is subjective and changes as a piece unfolds. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive way to study neural responses during listening, yet earlier work has mostly treated music emotion as a categorical label or relied on black-box models. We formulate enjoyment prediction as a regression problem on the public MUSIN-G dataset, which contains 128-channel EEG from 20 listeners together with song-level enjoyment ratings. Six deep learning models were compared under a participant-wise protocol, in which 15 listeners were used for training and validation and 5 were held out for testing. DeepConvNet, CNN-LSTM and GNN-CNN reached the lowest mean absolute error (0.97 to 0.99 on the 1 to 5 scale), while the temporal convolutional network (TCN) had the highest Pearson correlation with the ratings (r = 0.21). Gradient-based and occlusion-based explanations, averaged over all held-out windows, identify the time segments within each two-second window that most influence the TCN predictions. The study provides a reproducible cross-listener benchmark for EEG-based enjoyment regression and shows how explainability analysis complements standard metrics.
ai_summary: This research explores using EEG data to predict music enjoyment, which is challenging due to its subjective nature. The study found that deep learning models like DeepConvNet, CNN-LSTM, and GNN-CNN had the lowest mean absolute error in predicting enjoyment ratings, with the temporal convolutional network (TCN) showing the highest correlation. The use of explainability analysis in identifying time segments that influence predictions adds a new dimension to understanding neural responses to music enjoyment.

title: From Semantic Editing Intentions to Persistent Parametric Controls for AI-Assisted Image Editing
abstract: AI-powered image editing increasingly allows users to express high-level editing intentions, yet how these intentions are translated into concrete editing actions often remains difficult to understand. We present Atelier, a semantic image editing tool that uses image semantics and user intent to determine which editing controls to surface and how to initialize them. Guided by a formative study with eight image-editing practitioners, Atelier composes context-specific, directly manipulable controls that users can refine rather than committing AI interpretations directly to finished edits. In a within-subjects study with 12 practitioners, participants preferred AI-composed controls, described them as supporting creative exploration, and actively refined AI proposals. However, experiences of control were mixed, and interviews highlighted limited insight into why particular controls and values were proposed. Our findings suggest that making AI interpretations actionable through manipulable controls can support exploration and refinement, but actionability alone does not make those interpretations transparent to all users.
ai_summary: This research introduces Atelier, a semantic image editing tool that uses image semantics and user intent to determine which editing controls to surface and how to initialize them. Through a study with image-editing practitioners, it was found that users preferred AI-composed controls as they supported creative exploration and allowed for active refinement. However, users also expressed mixed experiences with control and limited insight into why particular controls and values were proposed, suggesting that while making AI interpretations actionable through manipulable controls can support exploration and refinement, transparency of these interpretations to all users remains a challenge.

title: Let Me Clarify: Interactive Modeling of Soft Attributes
abstract: People commonly express preferences through soft attributes such as is interesting,'' which are difficult to operationalize for computational preference modeling. Latent representations can obscure how such attributes are interpreted, limiting transparency and user control. We formalize softness as the diversity of valid interpretations a description permits and provide empirical support for this characterization. Our proposed measure estimates softness to guide clarification and determine when to generate computational approximations. This is instantiated in AttriFy, a mixed-initiative system that translates descriptions into executable Python functions over text corpora. An interactive dashboard connects the dialogue to proposed functions and computed values, enabling users to inspect, accept, reject, and refine interpretations. An exploratory within-subjects study with 32 participants compares our softness-guided clarification approach with an LLM baseline in supporting interpretable attribute construction. This work positions softness as a basis for constructing explicit, user-steerable attribute dimensions for downstream preference elicitation and decision-making.
ai_summary: This research focuses on modeling soft attributes, such as "interesting," which are difficult to quantify for computational preference modeling. The study introduces a measure of softness that estimates the diversity of valid interpretations a description can have, allowing for clarification and generation of computational approximations. The proposed approach, implemented in the AttriFy system, enables users to interactively translate descriptions into executable functions and make decisions based on interpretable attribute dimensions, enhancing downstream preference elicitation and decision-making processes.

title: What and Where in Identifying and Quantifying Conventions in Humans and AI Agents
abstract: Cooperative success rests in part on implicit communication. Partners converge on conventions: regularities that give an action meaning beyond its direct effect. Yet conventions are usually observed only indirectly: a score drop when partners are swapped shows that a convention existed, but not what it was or where it was used. In the card game Hanabi, the exact probability that a play fails can be computed from the hints received and the cards in view. Players who use conventions succeed more often than this prediction allows; the resulting margin is the convention gap. Off-belief learning provides a hierarchy of agents (levels 1-5) whose first level uses no conventions by construction and whose later levels use progressively more. For humans and these agents on one scale, we ask what the conventions are and where they are used. On what: in two independently collected corpora of human games, humans show a larger gap than every agent level. On the conventions both populations use, however, humans do no better than level 2. The human advantage is concentrated in a situation that no agent level learns to use: hints that point to a card other than the ones they touch. On where: conventions depend on what the player already knows about the card, not on how recently it was hinted, and they are used most in the mid-game; humans use them earlier and later in the game than the agents. In interventions on the agents, blocking a single high-gap situation costs little, because meaning reroutes to other situations, but blocking several together costs far more than the sum of the single costs. Thus, the convention gap turns conventions from an inferred cause of score loss into a measurable, comparable, and causally testable object.
ai_summary: This research examines the use of conventions in implicit communication between humans and AI agents during cooperative tasks, using the card game Hanabi as a case study. The study finds that humans outperform AI agents in utilizing conventions, particularly in situations where hints point to cards not directly touched. Conventions are found to be dependent on players' prior knowledge about the cards and are used most frequently in the mid-game. The study highlights the significance of conventions in improving cooperative success and provides insights for designing AI agents that can effectively use conventions in communication.

title: The Body-Algorithm-Emotion Loop: Making Emotion AI Misrecognition Visible through Artistic Practice
abstract: This pictorial presents The Body in Algorithmic Colonialism, a screen-based interactive installation that critically examines Emotion-AI through artistic practice. The work uses facial tracking to simulate how commercial Emotion-AI systems translate facial movement into emotional categories and verdicts of compliance or non-compliance. Rather than treating explainability as technical transparency alone, the installation approaches XAI as an embodied encounter with misrecognition: viewers experience how the body is measured, classified, and returned to itself through algorithmic thresholds. Drawing on critical AI studies, affect theory, and practice-as-research, the pictorial positions artistic practice as a method for making affective classification visible and contestable. It documents the conceptual framework, technical process, and critical context of a prototype developed in the first year of a practice-based PhD. No audience responses, interviews, or participant data are analysed in this submission.
ai_summary: This research explores the impact of Emotion-AI on individuals through an interactive artistic installation called The Body in Algorithmic Colonialism. The installation uses facial tracking to demonstrate how these systems categorize emotions and determine compliance. By engaging with the concept of explainability in AI and exploring the implications of emotional misrecognition, the research highlights the importance of artistic practice in making affective classification visible and open to critique.

title: Task-State Governance: A Virtual Machine for Verifiable and Recoverable GUI Agent Execution
abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents now execute workflows across real applications, but when execution drifts, users must determine what changed, what should have remained untouched, and what can still be recovered. Plan-centric interfaces leave users supervising procedure, but users live with changes to application state. We introduce task-state governance, an interaction paradigm that represents a task as an editable contract linking desired outcomes, facts that must be preserved, and observed application state. We instantiate this paradigm in TaskVM, which projects live state into editable task controls, executes user edits as genuine interface actions, verifies outcomes through independent observation, and marks each action as reversible, compensatable, or irreversible. Across an automated contract benchmark, a controlled user study, and an open live-model exploration, the paradigm strengthened contract compliance and users' recovery control and trust, while execution outcomes were held constant. Task contracts open a design space for governable agent interfaces.
ai_summary: This research introduces task-state governance as a new interaction paradigm for GUI agents executing workflows across real applications. The paradigm represents tasks as editable contracts linking desired outcomes, facts that must be preserved, and observed application state. The implementation of this paradigm in TaskVM allows for stronger contract compliance, improved user recovery control and trust, and marked actions as reversible, compensatable, or irreversible, ultimately opening up a design space for governable agent interfaces.

title: Scoping the Landscape of Large Language Model-based Affective Personal Informatics: Review, Reflection, Future Direction
abstract: Affective personal informatics (PI) involves capturing, tracking, analyzing, and reflecting on personal data to support emotional self-awareness and mental well-being. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) are reshaping affective PI, yet a comprehensive survey of LLM-based affective PI systems is lacking. To bridge this gap, we systematically analyzed 45 papers published between January 2020 and June 2026 across four major computing and health databases, examining their macro trends, system taxonomies, and research methodologies. Our synthesis reveals an overreliance on multi-stage, text-centric pipelines, a predominance of active, screen-bound interactions, and a severe demographic skew toward young, university-campus-based cohorts in empirical evaluations. Based on these findings, we critically reflect on prevailing architectural and methodological shortcomings and outline actionable future directions for building end-to-end multimodal, low-burden, and inclusive affective PI systems.
ai_summary: This research paper explores the use of large language models (LLMs) in affective personal informatics (PI) to support emotional self-awareness and mental well-being. The study found a lack of comprehensive surveys on LLM-based affective PI systems and identified trends in the field, including a focus on text-centric pipelines and a demographic skew towards young, university-based cohorts. The researchers suggest future directions for building more inclusive and effective affective PI systems that are multimodal and low-burden.

title: ShadAR: Real-time Prompting On-demand Visual Augmentation in Augmented Reality
abstract: Augmented Reality can reshape our visual perception (e.g., simulating color blindness) yet such effects are typically pre-programmed by experts, making visual augmentation static and inflexible. We introduce ShadAR, an AR system that allows users to describe expected visual augmentations (e.g., "Blur all people") for changing their vision in real time. ShadAR can graphically manipulate AR passthrough in real time via shader injection. When receiving a user's prompt, ShadAR uses LLMs (GPT5.2) to interpret the user's intent, analyzes the user's view with object detection (YOLOv26), generates a pixel shader, and applies it to the targeted region on AR passthrough. To understand usage patterns, we invited 21 HCI researchers to use ShadAR, identifying four application domains (design, health, productivity, and social interaction) and two prompt-framing patterns: procedural prompts specifying what to modify and how ("Highlight the book."), and end-goal prompts conveying desired mental or behavioral states ("Make me laugh."). Such end-goal prompts suggest a future in which users specify outcomes (e.g., "Make me not miss my flight") while the system determines how to realize them, though often with inherently indeterminate results. We discuss design opportunities for ShadAR and ethical concerns.
ai_summary: The research introduces ShadAR, an augmented reality system that allows users to describe visual augmentations in real-time, enabling dynamic changes to their visual perception. The system utilizes advanced technologies like language models and object detection to interpret user prompts and generate pixel shaders for real-time manipulation. The study identified potential application domains and prompt-framing patterns, suggesting a future where users can specify desired outcomes while the system determines how to achieve them, raising design opportunities and ethical concerns.
